title: When, Where, and Why Hippos Yawn: A Brief Analytical Report on Hippopotamus amphibius
content: Yawning is a behavior reported in many species of mammals. When a pod of hippos is observed in the evening, one usually sees many hippos yawn with their jaws wide-open. Despite yawning being a very evident behavior in hippos, we know of no major studies focused on the functions of this behavior aside from being an aspect of threatening encounters between adult males. This study focused on yawning in hippos with regard to the functions of brain activation and brain cooling. One study site was along the Luangwa River in South Luangwa National Park in Zambia which had a pod of approximately 40 resident hippos. A second site was at Plettenberg Bay Game Reserve in southern South Africa in July when the temperatures were cool, contrasting with the hot temperatures in Zambia. Only four hippos typically were present at the Plettenberg site. Observations pertained to two non-exclusive functions: that the brain is activated by yawning and that yawning cools the brain, contributing to brain activation. At Luangwa, the frequency of yawning greatly increased just before the hippos left the water in early evening to forage during the night: supporting both the brain activation and brain cooling functions. At Plettenberg, the hippos reclined on the riverbanks during cool days in July, but still yawned just before walking off, going into the river and moving upstream to forage. These data support the brain activation but not the brain cooling functions.
